extracted.intended_audience: The People of the State of New York (voters/citizens considering ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution)
extracted.subtask_short: advocacy for an energetic federal government
extracted.subtask_description: A series of persuasive constitutional standards arguing that the national government must be given sufficient, centralized powers (defense, judiciary, commerce, revenue, direct authority over individuals) to preserve the Union and prevent foreign corruption, local prejudice, and inefficiency. The text explains what powers are necessary, why limits or dispersed authority are dangerous, and offers practical examples and safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive supermajority requirements / prefer effective majority decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning that requiring the concurrence of a large number for national acts gives greater scope to foreign corruption and domestic faction, and can obstruct government at critical seasons; contrasted with permitting the sense of the majority to decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with the example of an ally who could more easily bribe enough members to prevent peace when two-thirds of all votes are requisite than when a simple majority would suffice. Explanation emphasizes that supermajority hurdles may prevent necessary good as well as block improper actions, and thus can be more dangerous than majority rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish one supreme tribunal to ensure uniformity of law
rubrics_metrics.description: "A circumstance which crowns the defects of the Confederation remains yet to be mentioned, the want of a judiciary power." Laws and treaties require courts to expound and define their meaning; to produce uniformity they ought to be submitted, in the last resort, to one SUPREME TRIBUNAL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If each State has a court of final jurisdiction there may be as many different final determinations as courts, producing confusion from contradictory decisions and local bias. The supreme tribunal should be instituted under the same authority that forms treaties and general laws to avoid infractions by different legislatures and judiciaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard the Constitution against foreign corruption and local partiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Republics afford an easy inlet to foreign corruption; persons elevated from the mass may be purchased by foreign emissaries, producing mortifying examples historically. A national government that rests on the consent of state legislatures leaves national interests at the mercy of local prejudices and passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (United Provinces, Sweden, deputies bought by neighboring kingdoms) are cited. To prevent such corruption the fabric of national government should rest on the consent of the people and on centralized institutions (e.g., a supreme tribunal and national authority) rather than on multiple state authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant federal powers coextensive with national exigencies (means proportioned to ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: The MEANS ought to be proportioned to the END; the federal government, entrusted with the care of common defense and national interests, ought to be clothed with all powers requisite to the complete execution of its trust because it is impossible to foresee or define the extent and variety of national exigencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No constitutional shackles should be imposed on the power to provide for defense, formation, direction, or support of national forces. If the Union is to manage particular national objects (defense, commerce, foreign intercourse), it must have all laws and regulations relating to them and not be hamstrung by inadequate authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal laws should operate directly on individuals (not via state requisitions/quotas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the 'fallacious scheme of quotas and requisitions'; the Union must extend its laws to individual citizens because legislating only upon the States in their collective capacities is impracticable and unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Confederation's reliance on requisitions failed (States frequently did not comply). For energy and duration, the federal government should have power to levy troops and raise revenues in customary modes practiced in other governments, rather than depending on state compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal control of military forces and revenue raising
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union ought to be invested with full power to levy troops; to build and equip fleets; and to raise the revenues required for formation and support of an army and navy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers should exist without limitation because of the infinite variety of circumstances that may affect public safety. The paper argues the national legislature—not the Executive—will hold the power to raise armies and that appropriations should be practicable in customary forms rather than by requisitions on states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate powers by object and give each power authority commensurate to its end
rubrics_metrics.description: If a compound (federal) government is adopted, discriminating the OBJECTS which shall appertain to different provinces or departments is essential; each should be allowed the most ample authority for fulfilling the objects committed to its charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not to confer in each case a degree of power commensurate to the end would violate prudence and entrust interests to hands disabled from managing them with vigor. Examples: national government should manage fleets and armies, states should manage administration of justice within states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common defense must be managed at the national level to avoid inequity and rivalry
rubrics_metrics.description: Territorial proximity of foreign powers and threats are common to the Union; to leave defense to the States would be oppressive to some, dangerous to all, and baneful to the Confederacy by imposing unequal burdens and producing jealousy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If certain states alone bear the burden of establishments (e.g., New York), others would be exposed or might counterbalance, producing mutual rivalry and oversized military establishments. Central management ensures equitable distribution of burdens and unified plans and measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic legislative appropriations (two-year limit) as a safeguard against standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of a constitutional prohibition of standing armies, the proposed plan contains a clause forbidding appropriation of money for the support of an army for any longer period than two years — a precaution that serves as a real security against keeping up troops without evident necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that precise constitutional interdictions would be impractical (how to define 'keeping up'?) and likely ineffectual. The two-year appropriation limit subjects military maintenance to frequent legislative oversight while leaving discretion to the legislature to meet genuine dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize practical necessity of small peacetime garrisons and naval infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanent corps in the pay of the government (small standing armies/garrisons) are sometimes indispensable in peace — e.g., frontier garrisons against Indian depredations, fortifications and garrisons for dock-yards and arsenals while a navy is in its infancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on the militia for continual rotations is impracticable and injurious (men will not submit to repeated service; it would burden private citizens and be costly). Moderate permanent garrisons and infrastructure are defensible for prudence and security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive national authority from the consent of the people (popular ratification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Confederation's infirmity arose partly because it never had ratification by the PEOPLE, resting only on the consent of several legislatures; the fabric of American empire ought to rest on the solid basis of THE CONSENT OF THE PEOPLE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ratification rests on state laws alone, it raises questions (e.g., legislative repeal of a compact). Popular ratification provides a deeper, more stable foundation for national government and prevents the ease of state-level revocation or obstruction of national interests.
